Below are general, widely accepted best practices for improving the energy efficiency of domestic hot-water systems. These recommendations are based on industry standards rather than any specific document evidence:

1. Optimize Heat Generation  
   • Install a high-efficiency heat pump water heater (HPWH). Its coefficient of performance (COP) can be two to three times higher than that of an electric resistance element.  
   • If using a boiler or combi-boiler, choose a condensing model. Condensing boilers recover latent heat from flue gases, boosting efficiency by up to 10–15%.  

2. Reduce Standby and Distribution Losses  
   • Insulate the storage tank with at least 50 mm of high-quality foam or blanket insulation to minimize standby heat loss.  
   • Wrap all hot-water pipes in closed-cell pipe insulation (13–19 mm thickness) to reduce distribution losses, especially in unheated spaces like basements or attics.  
   • Shorten hot-water runs by locating the tank near high-use fixture

An energy declaration (in Swedish “energideklaration”) is the report-style document you receive after an accredited energy expert has assessed a building’s energy performance.  In Sweden it takes the form of an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC), and typically includes:

• A building identifier (byggnadsid) and an EPC address ID (epc_idadr) to link the declaration to national and local registers.

• An energy class (epc_egienergiklass), graded from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient)—the latest class, if multiple are on record, is the one that applies.  
• A flag indicating whether it was owner-built (epc_egennybyggar).

While the EPC does not mandate exactly which household appliances you must buy, it sets the context for how efficient your appliances need to be in order to keep your building’s total energy use (and running costs) in line with its declared class.

Key considerations when selecting appliances in light of your building’s energy class:

1. Preserving a high energy class  
   - If your building already has a top EPC rating (A or B), it means heating losses and basic energy demand are low. To maintain that performance, choose appliances from the highest efficiency tiers (e.g. EU label A +++ or A on the current A–G scale). In Sweden, you always need two separate agreements in order to have electricity in your home: one with the network owner (grid contract, “nätavtal”) and one with an electricity retailer (supply contract, “elhandels- eller elleverantörsavtal”). They serve different purposes:

1. Grid contract (nätavtal)  
   • Party: the local grid‐ or distribution system operator (DSO).  
   • Purpose: to secure the right to transport electricity from the transmission network all the way to your property’s connection point.  
   • Components of cost:  
     – A fixed annual or monthly “effect fee” (to reserve capacity)  
     – A variable energy fee (per kWh) for losses and distribution  
     – Possible fixed customer fee  
   • Legal basis: regulated under the Swedish Electricity Act (1997:857) and overseen by the Energy Markets Inspectorate (Ei).  
   • Without this contract you cannot physically receive power—even if you have purchased electricity.

Load balancing in the context of electric-vehicle (EV) charging is the process of managing and distributing available electrical power among one or more charging points so that you never exceed the capacity of the supply connection. In practice, it ensures that multiple vehicles charging at the same time draw only as much current as the upstream wiring, transformer or utility agreement allows.  

Key aspects of EV-charging load balancing:

1. Why it’s needed  
   • Prevents circuit overloads and tripped breakers.  
   • Avoids costly upgrades to mains wiring or service panels.  
   • Ensures safe, reliable charging even when several EVs plug in simultaneously.  

2. Static vs. dynamic balancing  
   • Static load balancing allocates fixed power limits per charger based on a predefined schedule or wiring capacity.

According to the Swedish National Board of Housing, Building and Planning’s regulations (BBR 26, Chapter 6 on temperature requirements), stairwells and other common circulation areas in a building must be dimensioned so that their indoor air temperature never falls below +12 °C. This minimum ensures

• frost protection of building services (pipes, ductwork, etc.)  
• reliable operation of smoke control and pressurization systems  
• safe and comfortable egress in cold weather  

Habitable rooms (apartments, offices, etc.) are normally kept at +20 °C, but stairwells are expressly treated as non-habitable common parts and only require the +12 °C minimum.
